t.1.25.2: O best of the twice-born, come out quickly from my open mouth, for a brāhmaṇa is never to be slain by me, even one who is always given to evil deeds.
t.1.25.1: Sūta said: A brāhmaṇa, together with his wife, had reached his throat and was burning there like a blazing coal; to him the sky-ranger spoke.
t.1.25.3: To Garuḍa, who was speaking thus, the brahmin said: "This Niṣāda woman is my wife; let her come out together with me."
t.1.25.6: When that brahmin had come out together with his wife, the king of birds, swift as thought, spread his wings and flew up into the sky.
t.1.25.5: Then that brahmin came out, accompanied by the Niṣāda woman, and after blessing Garuḍa he went to the region he desired.
t.1.25.4: Take this Niṣāda woman with you as well and fly out quickly; quickly save yourself while you are not yet digested by my fiery heat.
t.1.25.7: Then he saw his father, and being questioned, he told his father: "I have been sent by the serpents and am set on bringing back the soma; to free my mother from slavery I shall indeed bring it today."
t.1.25.8: I have been instructed by my mother, "Eat the Niṣādas!" Yet, though I have devoured them by the thousands, I have found no satisfaction.
t.1.25.9: Therefore, O blessed one, point out to me some other food, by eating which I may become able to bring back the amṛta, O lord.
t.1.25.10: There was a great seer named Vibhāvasu, who was exceedingly wrathful. He had a younger brother, Supratīka, a man of great austerities.
t.1.25.11: That great sage does not wish to keep his wealth held in common with his brother; Supratīka, moreover, constantly speaks of nothing but partition.
t.1.25.12: Then his brother Vibhāvasu said to Supratīka: "Many, out of delusion, constantly wish to make a division of property; then, once divided, deluded by wealth, they do not respect one another."
t.1.25.13: Then, knowing these deluded men to be intent on their own interests and divided from one another by their own wealth, enemies in the guise of friends sow discord among them.
t.1.25.14: And others, knowing them to be divided, then fall upon them at their weak points; for those who are divided, unequalled ruin comes about very swiftly.
t.1.25.15: For that very reason the learned do not commend a division of property among those who, though bound by the teaching of their elders, are suspicious of one another.
t.1.25.17: Thus cursed, Supratīka then said to Vibhāvasu, "You too shall become a tortoise, moving about within the water."
t.1.25.16: Since you cannot be restrained and you desire the wealth through partition, therefore, Supratīka, you shall become an elephant.
t.1.25.18: Thus, through each other's curses, those two, Supratīka and Vibhāvasu, their minds deluded for the sake of wealth, came to be an elephant and a tortoise.
t.1.25.20: In this lake are two huge-bodied creatures, pursuing an ancient enmity; of the two, one, a splendid great elephant, is approaching.
t.1.25.19: Because of their clinging to the fault of wrath, even though both have passed into animal births, the two still delight in hating each other, proud of their size and strength.
t.1.25.21: At the sound of its trumpeting, the tortoise too, which lay within the water, rose up, that huge-bodied one, churning the entire lake.
t.1.25.22: Seeing him, this mighty elephant, his trunk coiled, plunges into the water with the force of his tusks, the tip of his trunk, his tail and his feet.
t.1.25.23: As he churned up the lake teeming with many fish, the mighty tortoise too, its head raised high, came forth against him for battle.
t.1.25.24: The elephant stands six yojanas high and is twice that in length; the tortoise is three yojanas in height and ten yojanas in circumference.
t.1.25.26: Having heard those words of his father, he of terrible speed, coursing through the sky, seized the elephant with one claw and the tortoise with the other.
t.1.25.25: These two, maddened by battle and each eager to conquer the other, you should quickly make use of; accomplish this task, which is your own desire.
t.1.25.28: Then those divine trees with golden branches, struck by the wind of his wings, trembled in fear, thinking, "May he not break us!"
t.1.25.27: Then the bird soared high up into the sky, and reaching Alambatīrtha, he approached the trees of the gods.
t.1.25.29: Seeing those trees with swaying limbs, whose shoots bore the fruit of every wish, the sky-ranger approached others whose forms and limbs were beyond compare.
t.1.25.31: There a rohiṇa tree, exceedingly tall and very great, spoke to him, the best of birds, as he came flying toward it with the swiftness of thought.
t.1.25.30: With fruits of gold and of silver were the trees whose branches were of beryl; he beheld those great trees, encircled by the waters of the ocean, shining brilliantly.
t.1.25.32: This great branch of mine, which stretches out a hundred yojanas, perch upon this branch and eat these two, the elephant and the tortoise.
t.1.25.33: Then the best of birds, impetuous, swooping down swiftly and shaking the tree, which was frequented by thousands of birds and whose body was like a mountain, broke that branch covered with dense foliage.
